unit.why: A short exemplum, copied from an older book (ס׳ מבחר/מבאר הפנינים), about a sage who did not worry over the sufferings of his people and explained this with a dream analogy. It sits inside a homiletic chapter on suffering.
unit.boundary_note: The text is garbled: an unrelated passage about festive meals, charity and the Shpoler Zeide's saying on giving a cup of whiskey is spliced into the middle of the exemplum, probably a layout or reading-order error. That passage is a teaching, not a story.

stories.start_quote: שפ"א היו אנשי מדינה אחת בצרה גדולה
stories.summary_en: When a country's people suffered harsh afflictions, one sage among them did not worry. Asked why, he answered that this world is like a dream and the world to come is the waking, so blows received in the dream will not hurt once he wakes.

tags.why: The narrative is a thin frame for a homiletic analogy, embedded in a chapter of teachings on suffering.
It praises the wisdom of an unnamed sage and is copied from an older book, though it is only mildly laudatory.

quotes: שהעוה״ז הוא דומה לחלום וטוה״ב להקיץ
tags.why: The world to come is the waking against which suffering in this world is weighed.
The story illustrates equanimity and acceptance of suffering.

missing_concepts: this world as a dream (as a metaphor, not a depicted dream)
